title: Trump, Biden and the importance of factual knowledge
author: Martin Skelton
summary: Skelton uses two news stories from summer 2024 to defend the place of factual knowledge in schooling. At the 2018 Nato summit Trump won an argument because he could cite accurate, agreed spending figures for every member country. In the Biden-Trump debate, Biden looked weak partly because he could not produce the facts that would have backed up his accusation. Skelton argues that the claim that everything is on the internet fails whenever we must build a position in the moment. He insists knowledge is the foundation for skills and understanding, while acknowledging that curricula must choose carefully which knowledge to make sticky to avoid overload. The piece is a short, newsy reinforcement of his wider case for knowledge learning.
points: Accurate, shared facts gave Trump's Nato argument real force, which shows that true knowledge held in memory is persuasive power rather than trivia.
The 'it is all online' defence of not learning facts only works when there is time to look things up and little at stake.
Knowledge acquisition is the base on which skills and later understanding are built, and it supplies the evidence for any argument we want to make.
Because there is far too much knowledge to learn, the real task is choosing what matters at each age without causing overload or leaving gaps.
quotes: On this occasion, Trump’s ‘facts on what every country was doing’ weren’t Trumpian fake facts. They were accurate. Because they were good facts - agreed and validated by everyone - they had a huge impact.

The valid criticism of Biden was that he didn’t know (or hadn’t made sticky) the facts that would help him win the argument against Trump. When he accused Trump of lying (not an outrageous accusation) he couldn’t produce the facts that would prove it so.

Whether this was because he didn’t ever know them or because his ageing has made them more difficult to be made sticky (even after a five-day Camp David preparatory session) doesn’t matter much for now. What does matter is that the absence of factual information to underpin his rebuttal of Trump made him look weak and contributed to him losing control of the debate.

I’m relating these two stories to re-emphasise the importance of learning knowledge in schools and life in general. The argument that all knowledge is on the internet (and, therefore we don’t need to bother learning it) works sometimes when we have time to look it up or when knowing something now doesn’t matter that much. It doesn’t work at all when we need it to support a position we are creating right now.

The big takeaway of both the Trump and Biden experiences is this: knowledge acquisition still matters hugely. It is the foundation of our skills development and, later, our deepening understanding. It provides evidence for arguments we might wish to make.

Because it matters so much, so do the right choices about what knowledge we want ourselves and our students to make sticky. Too much and we can hit overload. Too little and we can disable other important learnings from the start.
